original_question: Develop a stochastic search algorithm for Costas arrays that continues to work at larger orders of practical interest, especially orders 30, 31, 32, and 33.
target_in_paper: Section 5.3, Problem 13: "Develop a stochastic search method for Costas arrays which works in large enough orders of interest (in particular, in orders 30, 31, 32, and 33)."
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the paper's target as the stochastic-search open problem in Section 5.3 and preserves its emphasis on higher orders, especially 30, 31, 32, and 33 (Problem 13, p. 12).
missing_details: It should define what a Costas array/permutation is: a bijection f:[n] -> [n] such that all displacement vectors (i-j, f(i)-f(j)) for 1 <= j < i <= n are distinct (Section 3.1, Definition 1, p. 2).

It should specify that the task is a search problem for a fixed target order n, especially n in {30,31,32,33}, not a vague claim about 'larger orders of practical interest' (Section 5.3, Problem 13, p. 12).

It should reflect the nearby context that the intended search space is the permutation space on [n], and that the paper has in mind stochastic/genetic-style mutation-based search rather than exhaustive enumeration or an algebraic construction method (Section 5.3, pp. 11-12).

It should clarify what 'works' is meant to improve on: earlier stochastic searches were reported to perform adequately only in low orders and to fail to recover any Costas arrays above order 15 within about 1 hour (Section 5.3, p. 12).

If made fully stand-alone, it should say explicitly that the goal is to find a Costas array/permutation of the prescribed order, not to prove nonexistence, classify all arrays of that order, or solve the complexity question E(n) from Section 4.1.

If one wants to mirror the paper's immediate formulation more closely, one may mention the difference triangle T(f): the Costas property is equivalent to requiring that no row of T(f) contain a repeated entry (Section 3.4, p. 6).
No ambient ring/field, degree, homogeneity, or nilpotency conditions are relevant here; the setting is purely combinatorial, with variables ranging over permutations of [n].
refined_question: Develop a stochastic search method on the permutation space of [n] that, for target orders n in {30,31,32,33} and more generally for other sufficiently large orders of interest, successfully finds a Costas permutation f:[n] -> [n], meaning a permutation for which all displacement vectors (i-j, f(i)-f(j)) with 1 <= j < i <= n are distinct.
equivalent_formulation: Equivalent formulation (using the paper's difference-triangle criterion): develop a stochastic search method that, for n in {30,31,32,33}, finds a permutation f:[n] -> [n] whose difference triangle T(f), with rows t_k(f) = (f(j+k)-f(j) : j in [n-k]), has no repeated entry in any row.
justification: The draft is clearly aiming at Section 5.3, Problem 13, because it asks for a stochastic search procedure for Costas arrays and singles out exactly the same benchmark orders 30, 31, 32, and 33. The official problem itself is brief, so the needed precision comes from nearby context: the paper discusses genetic/random-mutation search over permutations, guided by a metric of deviation from the Costas property, and notes that previously tested stochastic methods broke down in higher orders, specifically above 15 within roughly one hour (Section 5.3, pp. 11-12). To make the question mathematically stand-alone, one must supply the definition of a Costas permutation from Section 3.1, and the difference-triangle reformulation from Section 3.4 is the one explicit equivalent formulation supplied nearby. The focus should remain narrow: this is a search-method problem, not the broader existence problem or the NP-complexity problem from Section 4. The benchmark orders are paper-faithful: Table 1 records known arrays in orders 30 and 31 and none known at 32 and 33 at the time of the paper (Section 3.3, pp. 5-6).

citations.label: equivalence of the Costas property with no repeated entries in each row of T(f)
